newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan MOF says to deal severely with DKB, Nomura.
newsitem.headline: Japan MOF says to deal severely with DKB, Nomura.

text.p: Japan will deal severely with Nomura Securities Co Ltd and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd for their links with a corporate racketeer based on the policy of preventing recurrences and re-establishing credibility, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference on Tuesday.
Asked when the penalties would be announced, Mitsuzuka said the ministry was in the final stages of preparing the penalties and he could only say that the announcement would be made soon.
Dai-Ichi Kangyo (DKB) was fined 500,000 yen by Tokyo Summary Court on Monday for hiding loans to a racketeer. It was the first time such a penalty has been imposed.
MOF is expected to announce administrative penalties this week against DKB and Nomura Securities in connection with a scandal involving payoffs to a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer.

Such racketeers typically buy shares in companies and try to extort money by threatening to expose dubious business practices, or are sometimes employed by firms to quash questions from legitimate shareholders at annual meetings.
Payoffs to sokaiya have been illegal since 1983, but many Japanese companies have found it difficult to cut off ties with the underworld.
Mitsuzuka also said Japan welcomes Thailand's moves to start discussions with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on how to help overcome problems in the Thai economy.
He said he had just heard that Thailand had started talks with the IMF on an economic coordination programme. "I welcome this," he said.
This would be the first step in an important move toward an overall economic package for Thailand, he said.
"I expect Thailand to be on a continued growth path and to regain trust from the financial markets as it moves toward reaching an agreement on such a programme," Mitsuzuka said.

Asked whether Japan would consider loans to Thailand through such organisations as the Export-Import Bank of Japan, Mitsuzuka said that in principle the Japanese government would cooperate with the IMF. "Should there be a new request from Thailand, we would consider it seriously," he said.

When the Thai finance minister and central bank governor visited Japan earlier this month they did not make any request for financial support from the Japanese government. The two countries agreed, however, to cooperate in the currency markets, including joint intervention to support the baht.
